claims.text: Near-equiatomic multi-element nanoparticles can form single-phase solid solutions with a high degree of atomic mixing.
The relevant nanoparticles can be synthesized by high-energy shock or chemical methods.
As-synthesized nanoparticles have an initially disordered microstructure with variable grain-boundary features.
Controlled post-synthesis annealing can selectively optimize grain-boundary character.
The annealing treatment can increase the density of thermodynamically stabilized grain boundaries without changing overall composition.
Grain-boundary density and atomic-scale boundary character govern the high-temperature stability of these nanoparticles.
Optimized grain boundaries impede atomic diffusion.
Optimized grain boundaries act as sinks for atomic diffusion.
Diffusion trapping or suppression at optimized grain boundaries reduces phase segregation and elemental drift.
Reduced phase segregation and elemental drift preserve the single-phase solid-solution structure during high-temperature exposure.
Relative to unannealed nanoparticles, grain-boundary-optimized nanoparticles will exhibit less elemental segregation.
Relative to unannealed nanoparticles, grain-boundary-optimized nanoparticles will better maintain phase purity.
Relative to unannealed nanoparticles, grain-boundary-optimized nanoparticles will undergo less structural coarsening.
The proposed mechanism applies to near-equiatomic multi-element nanoparticles across 473–1923 K, including catalytic operation at 773–1173 K.
The mechanism is conditional on annealing not causing significant oxidation or compositional change.
Surface oxidation may independently influence high-temperature stability.
